$$

I\!\left(\min(\hat{\beta}_s^{1r}, \hat{\beta}_s^{2r}) \geq 0\right).
$$

> **2026 note.** The rate is now evaluated in closed form from one fit of the
> working model within the candidate: to first order the two half-sample
> estimates are a mirror pair about the full-sample fit, so
> $p_{\text{cons}}(g) \approx \max\{0,\; 2\,\Phi((\hat\beta(g) - c_{\text{cons}})/\sigma_{D,g}) - 1\}$,
> with $c_{\text{cons}} = \log$ `hr.consistency` and $\sigma_{D,g}$ the robust
> (influence-function) standard error of $\hat\beta(g)$ (León and Anderson
> 2026b, Section 2.2; 2026a, Supplementary Section S3). Nothing is drawn:
> `consistency_method = "resample"` is the default and evaluates this
> expression, and `fs.splits` is used only where the closed form is
> unavailable for a candidate (a non-convergent fit, or a GLM effect it cannot
> represent), when the literal split-and-refit calculation runs as the
> fallback. The screen is complementary-pairs stability selection applied to a
> smooth estimating-function coefficient, which is why its rate has a closed
> form; passing at level $p^\star$ is the same as the one-sided
> $(1+p^\star)/2$ robust lower confidence bound for $\beta(g)$ clearing
> $c_{\text{cons}}$.
edits.basis: 2026b §2.2 (closed form; stability selection; z-test reading); 2026a S3; R/forestsearch_main.R roxygen for consistency_method (default 'resample', automatic fallback).

> **2026 note.** Multiplier resampling (`mr_inference = TRUE`), the
> post-selection inference of León and Anderson (2026a), reproduces this
> correction to first order on the enumerated family without refitting: one
> shared multiplier draw perturbs every candidate's effect through its
> influence values, the selection rule is re-applied to the perturbed effects,
> and the two-term de-biased estimate and the infinitesimal-jackknife variance
> above are read from a single matrix product (2026a, Sections 2.5 and 3;
> Theorem 1). It runs in seconds where the bootstrap runs in minutes (2026a,
> Section 6). The full bootstrap remains available as
> `forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture()` and is the reference on a fixed family;
> on a model-generated family (GRF, DINA) the two answer different questions
> (2026a, Section 5). The one-sided field bounds and the two-subgroup claim

> Section 3); the

The uniform-benefit (null) runs are the simulation estimate of a search's
declaration rate — the rate at which it declares some subgroup when the
treatment in fact benefits every patient. León and Anderson (2026a, Section 8)
recommend estimating that rate by simulation calibrated to the analyst's own
trial, using these data-generating mechanisms, and reporting it beside, but
distinctly from, the de-biased effect; 2026b (Section 4) adds the family-wise
size diagnostic of the executed screen, `fs_declaration_calibration()`, and
its Supplementary Section S1.8.4 compares the diagnostic with a realized rate
on a design of this kind.

edits.old: # Guidance for Choosing an Estimand
edits.new:
# The Post-Selection Target: the Standard Analysis of the Selected Region

The inference of León and Anderson (2026a, 2026b) targets the standard
analysis of the selected region: $\beta(\hat{H})$, the treatment coefficient
of the working model fitted within $\hat{H}$ — a Cox log hazard ratio for a
time-to-event outcome — and $\beta(\hat{H}^c)$ for the patients outside it.
It is the working model's least-false value, the value the coefficient
estimates whether or not the model is correct, with the candidate family held
fixed at what the data produced (2026a, Section 1.2 and equation 15). Three
properties matter for simulation work.

- **It is random across replicates.** $\hat{H}$ varies, so $\beta(\hat{H})$
  varies with it, and it is neither $\theta^\dagger(H)$, $\theta^\ddagger(H)$
  nor the AHR of the planted region. In the GBSG-based designs of 2026a its
  mean sits below the planted marginal hazard ratio, because the selected
  region absorbs patients from the complement (2026a, Supplementary Section
  S8.1).
- **It is the quantity the correction is built to cover.** The
  multiplier-resampling interval is characterized for $\beta(\hat{H})$
  (2026a, Theorem 2), and the field's one-sided bounds and the Bonferroni pair
  are stated for $\beta(\hat{H})$ and $\beta(\hat{H}^c)$ (2026b, Section 3).
- **Both families of targets are reported.** 2026a scores bias and coverage
  against the oracle refit on $H$, the marginal $\theta^\dagger$, the
  controlled direct effect $\theta^\ddagger$ and the conditional estimand
  $\theta(\hat{H}) = \exp\beta(\hat{H})$ (Section 7; Supplementary Section
  S8), and reports the mismatch between the true and the realized region as
  the identification factor $\kappa = \beta(H)/\beta(\hat{H})$; 2026b reports
  bias against the planted target separately (Supplementary Section S2.3).

The DGM-level quantities of this article therefore keep their role — they are
what a simulation plants and what classification is scored against — while
$\beta(\hat{H})$ is what the reported interval is about.


# Guidance for Choosing an Estimand

edits.old:
**Use AHR** as the default estimand for ForestSearch simulation studies.
It is deterministic, directly interpretable, and aligns with the
geometric-mean interpretation of treatment effect heterogeneity. The
AHR is a primary target when evaluating operating characteristics
(sensitivity, PPV, bias) across simulation replications.
edits.new:
**Use AHR** as the default *design* quantity for ForestSearch simulation
studies. It is deterministic, directly interpretable, and aligns with the
geometric-mean interpretation of treatment effect heterogeneity. It sets the
planted effect and is a natural target when evaluating identification
(sensitivity, PPV) and bias against the planted region across simulation
replications. For the inference reported on an identified subgroup the target
is $\beta(\hat{H})$, the previous section.

edits.old:
- The *true* treatment effects are defined through $\psi^0(z)$, a
  baseline causal quantity.
- Subgroup *selection* uses the Cox HR as an efficient screening tool.
- Subgroup *evaluation* uses the AHR and CDE, which avoid the
  conditioning-set problem.
- Bootstrap bias correction (`hr.H.bc`) and the decomposition of error
  into subgroup misidentification versus finite-sample noise provide
  further safeguards.
edits.new:
- The *true* treatment effects are defined through $\psi^0(z)$, a
  baseline causal quantity; the AHR and CDE summarize it over a region
  and are the truths a simulation plants.
- Subgroup *selection* ranks candidates on the within-subgroup Cox
  coefficient $\hat\beta(g)$, and the *reported* estimand is that
  coefficient's least-false value in the selected region,
  $\beta(\hat{H})$, corrected for selection by multiplier resampling
  (León and Anderson 2026a, Sections 1.2 and 3) — taken as the target by
  institutional choice, with the interpretive limits of a hazard ratio
  acknowledged (2026a, Section 8).
- Evaluation in simulations scores bias and coverage against both the
  planted quantities (AHR, CDE, marginal HR) and $\beta(\hat{H})$ (2026a,
  Section 7; Supplementary Section S8); the decomposition of error into
  subgroup misidentification versus finite-sample noise applies to the
  planted targets. The bootstrap bias correction of the 2024 workflow
  (`hr.H.bc`) is reproduced to first order by the multiplier correction
  (2026a, Theorem 1).

edits.section: Estimand Selection Guide — primary simulation estimand
edits.old:
**Primary simulation estimand: ForestSearch AHR.** Computed from AFT potential
outcomes as the geometric mean individual log-hazard difference, it is the
only hazard-ratio-scale estimand that achieves both individual-level and
population-level causal status (Fay & Li framework). It is unaffected by
conditioning-set distortion, deterministic given the superpopulation, and more
sensitive to early effects than RMST. From the WHI empirical evidence, this
sensitivity advantage is clinically material: AHR detected the breast cancer
risk elevation at 6 years while RMST required 12.
edits.new:
**Primary simulation design quantity: ForestSearch AHR.** Computed from AFT
potential outcomes as the geometric mean individual log-hazard difference, it
is the only hazard-ratio-scale estimand that achieves both individual-level
and population-level causal status (Fay & Li framework). It is unaffected by
conditioning-set distortion, deterministic given the superpopulation, and more
sensitive to early effects than RMST. From the WHI empirical evidence, this
sensitivity advantage is clinically material: AHR detected the breast cancer
risk elevation at 6 years while RMST required 12. It is the planted truth; the
inference reported for an identified subgroup is scored against
$\beta(\hat{H})$, the standard-analysis coefficient of the selected region,
as well as against the planted targets (León and Anderson 2026a, Section 7).
edits.basis: 2026a §7; the article's 'primary simulation estimand' reconciled with the manuscripts' coverage target.

edits.old:
**Applied reporting: CHR alongside AHR.** For applied output --- subgroup
hazard ratio summaries reported to clinical trialists --- the cumulative hazard
ratio $\log \hat{S}_1(t)/\log \hat{S}_0(t)$ is the most defensible
population-level causal estimand under non-PH (Fay & Li; Wei & Schaubel). The
nonparametric AHR of Prentice & Aragaki tracks this closely in practice and
adds useful time-averaged narrative.
edits.new:
**Applied reporting: the standard analysis, corrected for selection.** For an
identified subgroup and its complement the package reports the within-subgroup
Cox coefficient --- the analysis the trial would have run had the subgroup been
prespecified --- with the multiplier-resampling correction and one-sided
bounds (León and Anderson 2026a, Section 1.2; 2026b, Section 3). The choice is
institutional, not a claim of causal optimality: hazard ratios are
non-collapsible, and the corrected estimate inherits the interpretive limits
of the standard analysis (2026a, Section 8). Under non-PH the cumulative
hazard ratio $\log \hat{S}_1(t)/\log \hat{S}_0(t)$ remains the most
defensible population-level causal functional (Fay & Li; Wei & Schaubel), and
it or the nonparametric AHR of Prentice & Aragaki can accompany the reported
estimate as a time-averaged summary.

edits.old:
**GRF baseline covariate conditioning is theoretically justified.** Fay & Li
demonstrate that conditioning on more baseline covariates moves the Cox HR
estimand continuously from a population-level toward an individual-level causal
quantity. ForestSearch's GRF/LASSO covariate conditioning is not merely a
statistical procedure --- it is the mechanism by which individual-level
heterogeneous treatment effects become estimable and by which the frailty
aliasing illustrated in the vaccine efficacy example is resolved.
edits.new:
**Baseline covariate conditioning through the subgroup definition.** Fay & Li
demonstrate that conditioning on more baseline covariates moves the Cox HR
estimand continuously from a population-level toward an individual-level causal
quantity. A forest-search subgroup is a conjunction of baseline covariate cuts,
so its within-subgroup coefficient conditions on those covariates by
construction. The recommended candidate family is enumerated from the
covariates alone; a LASSO prefilter or a GRF or DINA generator makes the
selection correction conditional on the family it proposes (León and Anderson
2026a, Section 5), and the GRF variable-importance screen is removed as of
0.4.1.

edits.section: Estimand Selection Guide — per-replicate Cox HR
edits.old:
**Avoid interpreting per-replicate Cox HR causally.** The `hr.H.hat` column in
simulation results estimates the marginal Cox AHR, which under non-PH depends
on the censoring distribution, is not cleanly individual-level, and conflates
treatment effect with selection. Its divergence from `dgm$hr_H_true` quantifies
the combined selection bias, finite-sample noise, and censoring distortion.
edits.new:
**Avoid interpreting per-replicate Cox HR causally.** The `hr.H.hat` column in
simulation results estimates the marginal Cox AHR, which under non-PH depends
on the censoring distribution, is not cleanly individual-level, and conflates
treatment effect with selection. Its divergence from `dgm$hr_H_true` quantifies
the combined selection bias, finite-sample noise, and censoring distortion. The
selection part is what multiplier resampling removes: the corrected estimate
and its interval target $\beta(\hat{H})$, the least-false coefficient of the
realized region (León and Anderson 2026a, Section 3 and Theorem 2).

# What forestsearch Reports, Read Against This Review

The papers reviewed here concern the causal reading of a hazard ratio. León
and Anderson (2026a, 2026b) take a different question as theirs: how to
report, with valid inference, the effect of a subgroup the trial's own data
selected. Their target is the standard analysis of the selected region, the
within-subgroup Cox coefficient $\beta(\hat{H})$ and its counterpart
$\beta(\hat{H}^c)$ for the patients outside it --- the working model's
least-false value, by institutional choice: it is the scale on which trials are
designed and read, and "not a claim of causal optimality" (2026a, Section
1.2). The corrected estimate "inherits the interpretive limits of the standard
analysis"; hazard and odds ratios are non-collapsible (2026a, Section 8). The
AHR, CDE and marginal hazard ratio of the companion articles are
simulation-truth constructs, planted by a data-generating mechanism and used
to design simulations and to score identification; they are not the reported
estimand. Bounds are read by their location against the trial's own effect
and against clinically meaningful effect sizes, not as tests at the null
(2026b, Section 6.1).
